analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and replaces it with tax deductions, health savings accounts, and state high-risk pools.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 29 Republican cosponsors on the first day of the new Congress, never got a committee vote or floor action and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act — including its insurance rules, marketplace subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and the taxes that paid for them — effective January 1, 2018. In its place it would offer an income tax deduction for buying health insurance, expanded tax-advantaged health savings accounts, federal grants for state high-risk pools for people with preexisting conditions, and looser rules allowing insurers to sell plans across state lines under another state's laws. It would also let employers vary premiums based on wellness-program participation, create association health plans, and shield doctors who follow clinical guidelines from most malpractice claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income taxpayers would gain the most directly: the health insurance deduction and expanded health savings accounts are worth the most to people with tax bills to reduce and money to set aside. Healthy people buying individual coverage would likely see cheaper premiums because insurers could charge older and sicker customers more and sell lighter-benefit plans across state lines. Doctors and health systems would gain a safe harbor from malpractice claims when following clinical guidelines. Veterans with service-connected disabilities and Medal of Honor recipients could get care outside the VA system.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher earners, healthy enrollees, and physicians

how_it_helps.text: Creates an income tax deduction for health insurance of up to $7,500 per individual or $20,500 per family per year for people buying their own coverage [S3].

Expands health savings accounts: higher contribution limits, child health savings accounts, fitness equipment and dietary supplements counted as medical expenses, and bankruptcy protection for HSAs [S3].
Authorizes $2.5 billion a year in federal grants from 2019 through 2027 for state high-risk pools that would cover people with preexisting conditions after repeal [S3].
Lets insurers sell individual policies in any state under the rules of one designated 'primary state', ending the home-state consumer rules of every other state they sell in [S3].
Repeals the ACA's health-related provisions effective January 1, 2018, including its marketplace tax credits, Medicaid expansion incentives, and insurance taxes [S2].
Gives veterans with certain service-related disabilities and Medal of Honor recipients access to care outside the VA [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions would bear the largest cost: the bill strips key guaranteed-availability requirements and replaces ACA protections with high-risk pools funded at a level far below what repeal would remove, and pools like these covered only a few hundred thousand people nationally before the ACA. Lower-income households would lose marketplace tax credits that the deduction cannot fully replace, since a deduction is worth more to higher earners. Injured patients would face harder malpractice claims under the guideline safe harbor and mandatory review panels. People who do not join employer wellness programs could be charged up to 50% more in premiums and cost-sharing. Taxpayers fund the pool grants, and the loss of ACA revenue would add to deficits.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and lower incomes

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates several guaranteed-availability requirements in the individual insurance market and replaces the ACA's coverage guarantees with high-risk pools, which historically offered less comprehensive coverage and longer waits than the ACA market [S3].
The replacement tax break is a deduction, not a credit, so it is worth far more to higher-income households; the bill simultaneously ends the ACA's income-based marketplace subsidies [S2,S3].
Employers could vary premiums and cost-sharing by up to 50% of the plan's value based on wellness-program participation, effectively charging people with health conditions more [S3].

Doctors who follow federally recognized clinical guidelines would get a safe harbor from malpractice liability, and every health care lawsuit would face mandatory review by an independent medical panel before litigation — raising the bar for injured patients to recover [S2,S3].

The bill restricts the use of HSA funds for abortion except in cases of rape, incest, or danger to the woman's life, and includes a 'respecting human life' section further limiting abortion-related coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real help to self-employed and higher-income people buying their own insurance through the deduction and expanded HSAs, and its antitrust and Medicare-transparency provisions would give patients more pricing information. But the trade is steep: repeal ends federal help that millions of lower-income households rely on, replaces guaranteed protections for preexisting conditions with a grant program that historically covered far fewer people, and lets insurers sell plans written under another state's weaker rules. The benefits skew toward people who already have money or good health; the costs concentrate on those who do not.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to ten House committees on the day it was introduced and parceled out to several subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: H.R. 277 was introduced in the House on January 4, 2017, by Rep. David Roe of Tennessee and 16 other Republicans [S3].

It was referred the same day to ten committees — Energy and Commerce, Budget, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Natural Resources, House Administration, Rules, Appropriations, and Veterans' Affairs [S5].
In January and February 2017 it was referred to subcommittees on Health in three committees and to the Subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs [S5].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died at the end of the 115th Congress [S5].
All 29 of its cosponsors were Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the Affordable Care Act — those with preexisting conditions, lower-income marketplace enrollees, and Medicaid expansion beneficiaries — kept those protections, since the bill never advanced and the ACA remained in force through the 115th Congress. The bill's backers, including its insurance deregulation and malpractice-shield provisions, gained nothing.

industries.note: The bill would free insurers from several guaranteed-availability rules and let them sell plans nationwide under the loosest state's rules, while ending their ACA marketplace revenue stream; it also removes their federal antitrust exemption for health insurance. The deregulation gains would come largely by letting insurers charge sicker people more.

Doctors following federally sanctioned clinical guidelines would get a safe harbor from malpractice suits, with mandatory review panels and federal court jurisdiction before patients could recover. Providers also gain tax-advantaged payments through direct primary care arrangements.

The standard deduction and expanded HSAs concentrate tax benefits among people with enough income to owe taxes and to save; the bill also repeals ACA taxes that fell more heavily on high earners. This is a transfer paid for by ending subsidies that go to lower-income households.

industries.industry: Dietary supplement, fitness, and wellness industries
industries.note: The bill would let people pay for gym memberships, exercise equipment, vitamins, and supplements with pre-tax HSA funds up to $1,000 each per year, creating new customers for these industries.
Ministry members would be treated as covered by a high-deductible plan, making them eligible for tax-advantaged health savings accounts.
